title: What tools do you use to improve your Three.js renders?
author: Alone-Influence-3572
selftext:
Hey!  
I’m curious to know what tools you guys use to achieve high-quality visuals with Three.js.  
What does your workflow look like, and which tools do you rely on to make your 3D scenes look better and more realistic?  
I’m looking to improve the visual quality of my own projects, so I’d love to hear about the tools you use and your personal experiences.  
Thanks!

comments.author: Negative_Gur9667
comments.body: Start by making a screenshot of the scene and let Nano Banana or ChatGPT stylize it so you get an idea about what style you are going for.

replies.author: EC36339
replies.body:
I generally find it better to prototype directly with code (but outside my game's codebase). It's closer to the real thing and usually looks better, too.

Image generation is too fuzzy and inaccurate. Coding agents can produce you something that looks good, is interactive, and can be used in a game almost as it is.

comments.author: dgeisert
comments.body:
making them look better and making them more realistic are two different things.  I think my recent game looks good, but it isn't even slightly realistic:  
[https://dgeisert.itch.io/starry-meows](https://dgeisert.itch.io/starry-meows)

I find it is better to find an art style that fits the tools you are using than to try to force realism.

comments.author: EC36339
comments.body:
I don't use three.js, but here's how I'm currently improving all my procedural rendering code:

Phase 1: Inventory

Ask an agent to find out how things are currently working, what techniques are being used, messure performance as baseline.

Phase 2: Planning

* What visual features make this scene realistic?
* What rendering techniques can produce these visual features?
* What can be precalculated to improve performance?
* What visual features make this scene unique and SPECIFIC to the lore and mood of my game?

This is not just asking AI and going with whatever comes out of it, but an interactive process.

Knowing computer graphics helps. If you don't have the knowledge, this is where you learn as you go.

Phase 3: Prototyping

Vibe code a prototype with HTML and WebGL. Not sure if any three.js is involved in this, it's mostly the shaders that matter.

This is another interactive process. I need to give feedback and ask for improvements, and also pick and choose what visual features can be done in good enough quality and reasonable performance (or prevalculated without loss of quality).

Phase 4: Implementation

My game is written in C++, Slang and Vulkan. So no code from the prototype can be used directly.

Incorporating a visual feature into an actual game and engine takes a lot longer than vibe coding a prototype in JS. That's why phase 3 is important. For answering your question, this means that vibe coding JavaScript IS the tool.

The first Implementation should be real-time with minimal precomputation, so parameters can be tuned and baseline performance (before precalculation) can be measured.

Phase 5: Review, optimisation and refinement

Test, tune parameters, fix bugs, rinse and repeat.

Implement precomputation and measure performance again and compare quality. Tune parameters, fix bugs, rinse and repeat.

Phase 6: Diversify and generalize

Produce variations of the same effect or scene. See what needs to be made data driven. See what is reused across scenes or effects of different types and refactor, so it can be used to produce more effects.



So overall, this is not a question of tools, but of workflow. All I use for this is Claude Code and my build toolchain.

comments.author: Fuzzzy420
comments.body: Depending, if you use three.js purely as a renderer there are a couple ways. If you use three.js as a game engine, stop and switch to a proper engine 😜
